title: The imitators died first. The successors did not.
lede: Zima’s first competitors were other brewers’ clear malts, and none of them lasted. The products that took its market arrived seven years later with a spirits brand on the label.

blocks.title: Clear malts and what came after
blocks.subtitle: Zima, the copies of 1993–95, and the two products that later owned the shelf it opened.

items.name: Zima (Coors)
items.text: 1994 volume. Withdrawn in the U.S. in 2008; limited runs in 2017 and 2018; on sale in Japan.[^12][^14][^31]

items.name: Miller Clear
items.text: A clear beer tested in 1993. It never left its test markets.[^25] Slate: it “failed miserably.”[^13]

items.name: Clash (Stroh)
items.text: Tested in Colorado, New Mexico and Arizona from May 1994 as “the brewer’s answer to Zima.”[^19] Slate lists it among the me-too products that failed.[^13]

items.name: Zima Gold (Coors)
items.text: Coors’s own amber spin-off, launched nationally in May 1995 and withdrawn that summer.[^12][^3]

items.name: Smirnoff Ice
items.text: U.S. introduction. Slate says Zima “lost significant market share” to it. Still on shelves when Zima returned in 2017.[^20][^13][^25]

items.name: White Claw
items.text: 2019 volume, up from 11.3 million in 2018, in a hard seltzer market Nielsen put at about $1.5 billion.[^35]

blocks.source: Figures as cited. Miller also tested a clear malt called Qube in Providence and Sacramento, and Pabst had one called Izen Klar; we found no volume figures for any of the clear-malt rivals.[^12][^13] Units differ between rows (barrels and 2.25-gallon cases) and are not comparable.

blocks.title: Why the second wave won
blocks.body:
By 2002 the trade press was calling these drinks “malternatives” and counting as many as twelve brands expected by the end of the summer, most of them carrying a spirits name: Smirnoff Ice, Bacardi Silver, Skyy Blue. The three big brewers were expected to spend more than $350 million between them on marketing the category.[^20] Coors’s own entry that year was not Zima but a new fruit-flavored brand called Vibe, which Supermarket News reported it was preparing to launch.[^20]

Coors’s annual report for 2002 says Zima “was impacted disproportionately by the recent influx of new FABs in the United States.”[^8] Zima XXX in 2004 was an attempt to join them.[^9]

The category Zima opened is larger now than it ever was in the 1990s. Hard seltzers, which are also clear, lightly flavored and usually malt- or sugar-based, went from $496 million to about $1.5 billion in U.S. off-premise sales between 2018 and 2019.[^35]
